slides.text:
An array holds a fixed number of values, all of the same type, side by side. Its length is part of its type and never changes after it is created.

A list that grows is a different type, and it comes in a later course.
An element is reached by its index, counting from 0. The index goes in square brackets after the name.

exercises.title: Array and index
exercises.guide: Create an array and read its elements by position.

chunks.guide: An array holds a fixed number of values of one type.

notes.text: Square brackets, commas, one type for all.

chunks.guide: Read one element by its index. Counting starts at 0.

notes.text: The index goes in brackets. The first is 0.

chunks.guide: `{:?}` prints the whole array.

notes.text: Debug format: shows the brackets and commas.

exercises.title: Array type
exercises.guide: Write the type of an array, then ask for its length.

chunks.guide: The type has the element type and the length, in brackets.

notes.text: Element type, a semicolon, then the count.

chunks.guide: Decimals work the same way: type, semicolon, count.
`len` returns how many elements the array holds.

notes.text: Counts the elements without you counting them.

chunks.guide: Three scores means the last one is at index 2. Four temperatures, index 3.

exercises.title: Fill the type
exercises.guide: Complete the type, then the two reads of the readings.

exercises.title: What does it print?
exercises.guide: Read the code, then pick the output.
exercises.explanation: The first score is `scores[0]`, 72. The length is 4, so the last is `scores[3]`, 64. The sum is 136.

exercises.title: Repeat a value
exercises.guide: Fill an array with the same value without listing it.

chunks.guide: Write the value, a semicolon and the length.

notes.text: Five copies of 0. No need to list them.

chunks.guide: Any value works, a `bool` for example.
Print both arrays.

exercises.title: Prices and the last item
exercises.guide: Read the first and the last price of an order.

chunks.guide: Five item prices.
The last index is the length minus one, so it never has to be counted by hand.

notes.text: Length is 5, so the last index is 4.

chunks.guide: Print labeled lines: the count, both ends and their sum.

exercises.title: Update in place
exercises.guide: Use an element in operators and compound assignment.

chunks.guide: Three counters. An array can change only when its variable is `mut`.
Operators like `+=` work on one element. An element can also feed another.

notes.text: Reads one element to compute another.

chunks.guide: Print the counters.

exercises.title: Book the seats
exercises.guide: Book the last seat and the middle one.

exercises.title: Named positions
exercises.guide: Name each position of a ports array with a constant.

chunks.guide: A constant holds a position. Indexes are `usize`.
Ports in the same order as the constants.
The constant works as the index.

notes.text: Same as ports[1], but it says what it means.

chunks.guide: The array must be `mut` to be rearranged.
`swap` exchanges the elements at two indexes.

notes.text: Takes two positions, not two values.

chunks.guide: Print the swapped array.
`reverse` flips the whole array.

notes.text: Changes the array itself, returns nothing.

chunks.guide: Print it again.

exercises.title: What does it print?
exercises.guide: Read the code, then pick the output.
options: It does not compile: `a` is unusable after `b = a`
exercises.explanation: An array of integers is copied when assigned, so `b` is a separate array. Changing it leaves `a` alone.

exercises.title: What happens?
exercises.guide: This program builds. Read it, then pick what happens when it runs.
exercises.explanation: The length is 3, so `i` is 3, but the last index is 2. The program builds, because the index is only known at run time. Then it panics with index out of bounds, and never reads past the array.

slides.text:
An array can hold arrays. The outer array holds the rows, and each row is an array of columns. Two indexes reach one cell: the row first, then the column.

The snippet is pseudo code, not Rust.
slides.code:
table = [ row0, row1 ]
row0  = [ cell, cell, cell ]
table[1][2]  ->  row 1, column 2

exercises.title: Length from a constant
exercises.guide: Size an array with a constant.

chunks.guide: A constant can give the length of an array.
The length must be known when compiling, so a normal variable cannot be used here.

notes.text: The constant stands where a number would.

chunks.guide: Check the length and the content.

exercises.title: Arrays inside arrays
exercises.guide: Build a table: an array of rows.

chunks.guide: An array can hold arrays. Here, two rows of three numbers.

notes.text: Two rows, each an array of three i32.

chunks.guide: The first index picks the row, the second the column.

notes.text: Row 1 first, then column 2 inside it.

chunks.guide: Print the whole table.

exercises.title: Size the table
exercises.guide: Fill the two lengths in the type of the table.

exercises.title: A grid of zeros
exercises.guide: Repeat an array inside a repeat, then edit cells.

chunks.guide: Repeat a row to build a grid: two rows of four zeros.
A cell takes two indexes, row then column.
Print the grid.

exercises.title: What does it print?
exercises.guide: Read the code, then pick the output.
exercises.explanation: `grid.len()` counts the rows, which is 2. `grid[0]` is one row, and its length is 4.

chunks.guide: Three arrays: the third has the same elements in another order.
`==` compares two arrays element by element, in order.

notes.text: True when every position holds the same value.
